name: Ilarion of Kyiv
otherNames: Hilarion, the form of S. H. Cross's English
Larion, the form of the Laurentian copy's entry for 1051
knownFor: A priest at Berestovoye who dug the cave where the Caves monastery of Kyiv began. In 1051, the Russian Primary Chronicle says, Prince Yaroslav of Kyiv gathered the bishops and made him metropolitan of Rus. He left a confession of faith in his own name, and the 1844 Moscow edition argues that he wrote the Sermon on Law and Grace.
dates: Made metropolitan in 1051, the year 6559 from the creation of the world, by the Russian Primary Chronicle and his own confession of faith. Michael Harasiewicz's Annales Ecclesiae Ruthenae (1862) gives 1031 for the election, as the scan reads twice, and dates the next metropolitan, George I, to 1063. No source used here gives his birth or states the year of his death. The 1844 foreword places the Sermon after 1037 and before the death of Yaroslav's wife Irina in 1050, and notes that by 1079 another metropolitan, George, is named. The Chronicle in Cross's English names Metropolitan George earlier, in its entry for 1072
place: Berestovoye, where he was a priest at the church of the Holy Apostles, a village near the present Caves Lavra with the grand prince's palace, the 1844 foreword says; the wooded hill by the Dnieper where he dug his cave, later the site of the old Caves monastery; Saint Sophia in Kyiv, where he was made metropolitan
role: Presbyter at Berestovoye; metropolitan of Kyiv; author of a confession of faith and, the 1844 foreword argues, of the Sermon on Law and Grace

keyWorks.title: Confession of faith
keyWorks.about: signed by Ilarion as a monk and presbyter, made metropolitan in Kyiv in 1051 under the faithful Kagan Yaroslav. It follows the Nicene Creed in one manuscript. The 1844 foreword says there is no doubt it is his. Kagan was a ruler's title, a note in that edition says, taken from the Khazar lords who once held southern Rus

keyWorks.title: Sermon on Law and Grace
keyWorks.about: with a praise of Prince Vladimir, Yaroslav's father, and a prayer to God from all the land. It sets the law, pictured as Hagar the slave, beside grace, pictured as Sarah the free woman, and near its end calls Vladimir from his tomb to see his son and his city. The 1844 foreword argues it is Ilarion's, and says three of the four copies it saw lack the closing address to Vladimir

keyWorks.title: The prayer from all the land
keyWorks.about: the sermon's closing prayer, which the 1844 foreword counts as part of it. The foreword says a prayer named as Metropolitan Ilarion's, for the tsar and all Orthodoxy, was ordered read in 1555, as Archbishop Gurii went to Kazan, and takes it to be this one

traces: The Russian Primary Chronicle says Antony of the Caves, home from Mount Athos, settled on the hill where Ilarion had dug his cave. The Caves monastery grew there.
S. H. Cross says the Bible passages in the Chronicle's speech of the Greek missionary to Vladimir are borrowed from the Sermon, citing Sreznevski.
The 1844 foreword says a chronicler of Volhynia, late in the thirteenth century, reused the Sermon's praise of Vladimir for Prince Vladimir Vasilkovich.
remembered: The Chronicle calls him "a virtuous man, learned and ascetic."
The 1844 foreword says some lists of Rus saints count him among the holy men of Rus, though no record shows that the whole Russian church accepted this.
A. N. Mouravieff, a Russian official writing in 1838, calls Ilarion's cave the germ of the future Lavra, the Caves monastery, and of all the religious houses of Russia.

uncertain: His life is thin. It rests on two entries in the Russian Primary Chronicle and on his own confession of faith. The 1844 Moscow edition gives the Chronicle passages and says this is all that is known of him. No source used here gives his birth or states the year of his death.

Who wrote the Sermon. The 1844 foreword argues it is Ilarion's: in one manuscript it runs on in one hand into the Creed and his confession; it calls Vladimir and Yaroslav Kagan, as the confession calls Yaroslav; and its prayer matches one read in 1555 under his name, if, the foreword says, that guess is right. S. H. Cross calls it attributed to Ilarion.

When the Sermon was given. The 1844 foreword places it after the church of the Annunciation at the Golden Gate, which the chronicle it cites puts under 1037, and before Irina died in 1050, since it prays for her and for Yaroslav as living. The Chronicle in Cross's English gives the princess's death on 10 February, in an entry for 1048 to 1050; the Laurentian copy sets it under 1050.

Why he was consecrated in Kyiv. The chronicler does not say why Yaroslav did not send him to Constantinople, as the 1844 foreword notes; it holds that Yaroslav did not mean to break the Kyivan church's tie to Constantinople. A. N. Mouravieff blames Yaroslav's anger at the emperor Constantine Monomachus for blinding Rus prisoners, and says Ilarion soon won a letter of blessing from the patriarch Michael Keroularios. R. W. Blackmore, his translator, reports that the historian Karamzin praised Yaroslav's wisdom, since Yaroslav suspected the emperors might use the Rus church's dependence for their own ends. Jacob Susza, a bishop in union with Rome, quotes the archbishop Meletius Smotrytsky in a book of 1666. Smotrytsky says that in 1051 Rus would not take its metropolitan's consecration from Michael Keroularios, whom he calls the leader of the schism.

A man of Rus. The Laurentian copy calls him a Rusin, a man of Rus, and the 1844 foreword concludes that he was Russian by birth. Cross's English reads "Metropolitan of Rus". A. N. Mouravieff calls him and Clement of Smolensk, a later metropolitan, the native Russian metropolitans.

Who made him a monk. In his confession he calls himself a monk and presbyter. Simon, bishop of Vladimir and Suzdal, in his letter to the Caves monk Polycarp kept in the Caves Paterik, says Polycarp had read in a Life of Saint Antony that Antony tonsured Ilarion. That Life is not among the sources used here. The Chronicle has Ilarion dig the cave before Antony came. The Caves Paterik's founding account brings Antony to Kyiv earlier, before Ilarion dug his cave. Antony lived at Berestovoye, in a cave that Varangians had dug. After Vladimir died, Prince Sviatopolk began killing his brothers, and Antony fled back to Mount Athos.

His end. The chronicler does not say how long he led the church, the 1844 foreword notes, and another metropolitan, George, is named by 1079. The Chronicle in Cross's English names Metropolitan George in its entry for 1072, and Mouravieff says George was sent early in the reign of Izyaslav, Yaroslav's son. Michael Harasiewicz's list of the Kyiv metropolitans (1862) puts George I in 1063. Mouravieff reports that several writers guessed Ilarion took the name Ephraim with the great monastic habit, and bore it when he died. S. H. Cross, reporting A. A. Shakhmatov, says later versions moved the Caves passage back to 1051 "to connect it with the death of the metropolitan Hilarion". No other held line ties his death to that year, in which the Chronicle has him made metropolitan.

Who wrote the Chronicle's passage on the cave. The 1844 foreword gives it as the Venerable Nestor's. Sylvester, prior of Saint Michael's, says he wrote the Chronicle in 1116. Cross reports that A. A. Shakhmatov ascribes this passage to Nikon, a monk of the Caves, and thinks it first stood under 1062 and was later moved back to 1051. Cross himself argues against the tradition that Nestor wrote the Chronicle. The Caves Paterik's founding account tells the passage on Ilarion's cave in nearly the same words.
